meta.title: Political economy knowledge network, c. 1962-2026
meta.description: Key works and debates in political economy: institutions and long-run development, history, culture and persistence, state capacity and taxation, inequality and redistribution, welfare states, varieties of capitalism and growth models, central banks and fiscal institutions, political business cycles and economic voting, interest groups and rent seeking, political agency and accountability, corruption, finance and crises, labor and unions, development and distributive politics, regimes and economic performance, and media and information. Seeds come from this repo's papers.json via the comparative politics and IPE maps; works shared with the other maps are imported from them; others are top-cited 2006-2026 articles selected via Crossref (economics and political-economy journals plus political science journals) and anchoring books and classics. Direction: source (later or dependent work) -> target (earlier or anchoring work).

edge_types.builds_on: source extends or relies on target's argument or evidence
edge_types.challenges: source contests target's claim, mechanism or evidence
edge_types.qualifies: source adds a scope condition or moderating factor to target
edge_types.extends_to_new_case: source applies target's logic to a new population, period or domain
edge_types.synthesizes: source integrates target with other work
edge_types.mechanism_tested_by: source tests a mechanism implied by target

meta.verification: Repo works come from the user's Zotero library. Works imported from the other maps keep their verification. Crossref-selected works take title, authors, year, venue and DOI from Crossref records. Anchors are checked in Crossref separately; see each node's `verified` field. One-line claims for non-repo works are my summaries.

edges.why: Generalizes the credible-commitment account of England's Glorious Revolution into a theory of institutions.
Colonial settler mortality as an instrument for institutions.
Endowments shape institutions in the Americas.
Like Engerman and Sokoloff, traces modern development to the institutions colonizers set up.
Develops the self-reinforcing institutions framework of Greif and Laitin into a book-length account of medieval trade.
Democratic institutions lower political risk for FDI.
Adds to evidence that political risk and institutions shape FDI, stressing democratic constraints on expropriation.
Slavery's political legacy in the U.S. South.
National institutions matter little within groups.
Origins of fiscal and legal capacity.
Extends Barro-style cross-country growth regressions to government size and spending volatility.
Race and institutions, not the median voter.
Shifts the inequality debate from top-income shares to intergenerational mobility across U.S. places.
Business power limited U.S. social policy.
Two facets of social policy preferences.
Party politics and the welfare state.
Globalization did not end partisan politics.
EU integration and social market economy.
Infrastructural power of finance over central banks.
Shows rational political budget cycles are larger where fiscal transparency is low and polarization high.
Tests in Mexico the institutional argument that corruption erodes generalized and political trust.
Political economy of the mortgage crisis.
Argues banking systems reflect political bargains among coalitions rather than inherited legal origins.
Traces rising German wage inequality to growing pay differences across workplaces as collective bargaining weakened.
Applies the commuting-zone exposure design of the China-shock study to industrial robots.
Reviews randomized field experiments in development economics, including Olken's audit experiment on corruption.
Tests whether the authoritarian legislatures Gandhi theorizes constrain rulers and raise growth and investment.
Shows radio access made New Deal spending more responsive to informed voters, paralleling Besley-Burgess on media and responsiveness.
Argues macroeconomic policy follows partisan class targets (left: low unemployment, right: low inflation) rather than a common opportunistic pre-election cycle.
Shows retrospective economic voting is strong only where clarity of responsibility is high, a cross-national scope condition on reward-punishment voting.
Generalizes clarity of responsibility into a competency-signal model of how political and economic institutions condition the economic vote.
Reviews the sociotropic-versus-pocketbook debate opened by Kinder and Kiewiet within a broader assessment of retrospective voting's competence.
Registry-measured personal income changes move votes, contesting the claim that voters respond only to national economic conditions.
Answers the measurement problems Healy and Malhotra flag in survey self-reports by using administrative income data to identify retrospective voting.
Places China-shock evidence on local labor markets within a broader review of how economic shocks reach voting, stressing cultural mediation.
Extends the author's Great Recession evidence on shock-driven welfare preferences into a general account of political responses to economic shocks.
Shows delegation to a conservative central banker is credible only when veto players make it costly for governments to override the bank.
Finds the inflation benefits of legal central bank independence appear only in countries with multiple political checks.
Shows grant-financed subnational governments with borrowing autonomy face soft budget constraints, undermining the market-preserving federalism mechanism.
Finds CBI reforms are followed by financial deregulation and credit booms, contesting the view that independence is a cost-free route to price stability.
Argues transformative institutional change often occurs through gradual layering and drift, contrary to Hall's view that fundamental change comes as punctuated paradigm shifts.
Argues generalized trust stems from economic equality and universal welfare institutions rather than from dense civic associations.
Develops the claim that impartial, universal institutions generate trust into an institutional theory centered on street-level bureaucracies.
Shows that where rents are large and parties weak, reelection incentives fail to discipline mayors and corrupt incumbents are voted out instead.
Tests the Weberian meritocracy mechanism, finding regions where bureaucrats' careers are insulated from politicians have lower procurement corruption risk.
Uses the single-bidder procurement risk indicators developed by Fazekas and Kocsis as its outcome measure.
Responds to the gap between corruption perceptions and reality by constructing objective red-flag indicators from contract data.
Meta-analysis finds near-zero vote effects of corruption information in field experiments, in contrast to the large effects of released audits in Brazil.
Shows that the hope that informed voters punish bad governance holds in observational designs but not in most randomized information interventions.
Tests the revenue-bargaining mechanism, finding that taxes high relative to services, not tax levels per se, predict democratization.
Extends the taxation-representation link into a fiscal-contract theory in which different taxpayer groups receive different public goods.
Experimentally tests whether tax-funded budgets make citizens monitor and sanction officials more than windfall-funded budgets.
Provides micro-level evidence for the claim that nontax revenue weakens citizen pressure on government spending.
Shows representative assemblies could constrain rulers only in geographically small polities, a scope condition on parliamentary commitment.
Shows that access to cheap foreign credit let rulers fight wars without building tax capacity, breaking the war-makes-states link.
Adds external finance as a substitute that lowers the return to fiscal capacity investment in the Besley-Persson framework.
Tests whether elite cohesion over common interests drives fiscal capacity, using the balance between landed and industrial elites.
Extends fiscal centralization and constraints in European public finance into a broader account of which elite coalitions build tax capacity.
Identifies weakened bureaucratic capacity after Reconstruction as an institutional channel through which slavery's legacy persisted in the South.
Argues retrenchment proceeds through hidden drift as programs fail to cover new risks, so formal program stability masks declining protection.
Extends Hacker's hidden politics of social policy to tax expenditures that obscure the state's role from citizens.
Shows welfare regress followed partisan and class lines, contesting the claim that retrenchment politics is decoupled from the power of the left.
Applies power resources theory to the retrenchment era, using replacement-rate data to show left power still shapes social rights.
Argues welfare expansion responded to deindustrialization-driven labor-market risk, not to trade openness as in the compensation thesis.
Finds external risk from openness explains little of welfare growth once domestic sectoral shifts are accounted for.
Recasts the three welfare regimes as distinct trade-offs within a service-economy trilemma of fiscal restraint, equality and employment.
Shows that for insurance-type spending, rising inequality lowers rather than raises support, reversing the Meltzer-Richard prediction.
Tests the social-insurance model on disaggregated spending categories, confirming inequality lowers support for insurance programs.
Shows tax preferences are shaped by fairness beliefs and settle on modest top rates, not simply by voters' position in the income distribution.
Extends findings that unions compress wages to the cross-national level, showing centralized wage-setting explains differences in pay inequality.
Reviews how the decline in unionization documented by Western reduces workers' political voice and contributes to rising inequality.
Integrates insider-outsider divisions into a review of whether unions still represent the broader working class.
Adds machine monitoring of individual votes to swing- versus core-voter targeting models of distributive politics.
Reviews empirical tests of the swing-voter and core-voter targeting predictions derived from Dixit and Londregan.
Reassesses the machine-politics literature following Stokes, arguing for focus on brokers and credibility rather than monitoring alone.
Argues the vote-buying versus turnout-buying distinction is often a red herring because both strategies coexist within broker networks.
Tests the media-capture mechanism by showing billionaires buy outlets as political investments and shift coverage toward their interests.
Reviews the historical-persistence agenda and argues it needs explicit theories of how effects are transmitted across generations.
Uses the mita study as an exemplar while cautioning that spatial discontinuity designs leave transmission mechanisms underspecified.
Argues Britain's credible borrowing after 1688 depended on creditor representation within the Whig coalition, not constitutional checks alone.
Shows land redistribution is more common under autocracy than democracy, contrary to the view that democratization brings redistribution.
Contests the link between democracy and redistribution by showing autocrats split from landed elites expropriate land at large scale.
Extends the varieties of capitalism framework to explain how democracies shape and sustain the knowledge economy.
Argues democratic capitalism is resilient because middle-class voters support the knowledge economy, contrary to accounts of crisis and capture.
Argues voters select good types rather than sanction shirking, because retrospective sanctioning is not credible when politician types differ.
Reviews electoral accountability models, organizing them around Fearon's distinction between selection and sanctioning.
Explains Cameron's openness-government size correlation as governments providing social insurance against external risk.
Shows the compensation logic fails in developing countries, where weak labor cannot defend welfare spending under globalization.
Argues that strong left parties with encompassing unions can sustain redistribution despite capital mobility, extending power resources theory.
Extends the partisan theory of macroeconomic policy to the era of financial globalization.
Argues nontax revenue stabilizes democracies as well as autocracies by funding redistribution, so oil does not hinder democracy per se.
Using long historical series and within-country variation, finds no evidence that resource reliance promotes authoritarianism.
Shows insider-outsider dualization of labor markets and social protection is a general trend across deindustrializing societies.
Shows the declining working-class vote reconfigured welfare support coalitions toward middle-class voters, loosening the class basis of welfare politics.
Provides evidence for the realignment of welfare state coalitions reviewed in Häusermann et al.
Applies the China-shock design to Western European regions, linking import competition to support for nationalist and radical-right parties.
Reviews European import-shock evidence on nationalist voting alongside US findings.
Shows workers in routine, automatable jobs demand more redistribution, extending risk-based theories of social policy preferences.
